objects.text: How do I brief an AI tool and check what it returns?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 3 of 12
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session you saw four cases where an assistant was tested, and you wrote the checks for your own task. Today I show you the same email written from a weak prompt and from a strong brief, with every figure recounted, and then you write the brief for your own task on paper.

The question for today is this: How do I brief an AI tool and check what it returns? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

Three parts matter most today. I spend twenty-five minutes on tools, account questions and the seven parts of a brief. Then thirty minutes on the two prompts and their results. After the break, thirty-five minutes are yours: you write your brief on paper and plan how you will check its result.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  How does an assistant produce an answer, and why can it be fluent and wrong?
2.  Name the four failures from Session 2 and the control for each.
3.  In the handbook case, which two questions could the document not answer, and what did Claude do?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 2. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. How does an assistant produce an answer, and why can it be fluent and wrong? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. It writes a likely next word from patterns learned in training and is tuned to help. Unless search, files or memory are on, nothing in that process checks a fact.

Question two. Name the four failures from Session 2 and the control for each. Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Made-up facts: open every source. Beyond the document: give the document and allow not stated. Sources disagree: ask for both figures. Wrong sums: recount in a sheet.

Question three. In the handbook case, which two questions could the document not answer, and what did Claude do? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. Paid sick days and the rate a kilometre for a private car. In both runs Claude wrote not stated. It had been told it could.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
First, the words I use all day. A prompt is anything you type. A brief is a prompt written once, in seven parts, and reused. The assistant is the product you talk to, and the model is the engine inside it. Assistants come in four common kinds. Chat only, which answers from the conversation.

With files, which reads documents you attach. With search, which can look things up on the web. And with saved instructions, which some tools call projects or custom assistants. Check which your account offers. Until your policy in Session 9, put nothing from your company into a tool.

slides.notes:
This is the structure of your brief, taken from your template. Goal, context, inputs, constraints, format, how I will check, and what to write when unsure. Part seven is the line that tells the tool what to do when it cannot support a claim. In our strong email it said the data does not show why volumes rose.

Part six is different. It is a note to yourself about what you will compare before you send, so it is not an instruction to the tool. You write the brief once, check it, and reuse it. Next time you change only the inputs. Now I show you what these parts did for one email.

objects.text: Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden. One run each.

slides.notes:
Here is how the two results were made. Both prompts carried the same data: total revenue, units and revenue for five products, for the weeks starting the twelfth and the nineteenth of October. The weak prompt was one line, write the Monday sales email, plus the data. The strong brief was one hundred and fourteen words.

I gave each to Claude as a fresh session that was given only the prompt and told to use no other tool or file, except to save its answer, with no answer key. I cannot prove from outside that it used nothing else. I ran each only once.

This is Claude, not ChatGPT or Gemini. One run each is a small sample, so I do not call the result typical, and another product or another day may differ.

slides.notes:
Here are extracts from the two emails, side by side. On the left, the weak prompt. The weak prompt gave no reader, so it wrote to the team, although the real reader is a director. It ends with advice to keep stock of beans and sugar high because demand is rising, which two weeks of data hardly support and nobody asked for.

And it signs off with a placeholder, your name. Red shows what the strong brief settles or forbids. It does not say the weak prompt broke an instruction. On the right, the strong brief. It writes to Sarah, it says the data does not show why volumes rose, and it ends with one thing to check, as the brief asked.

These are extracts from one run each, and I show you the figures after this.

objects.text: Recomputed from the data in the request. Claude, fresh session, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden, 1 run each.

slides.notes:
I recomputed every figure in both emails from the data. The total is right in both. The change on the week is thirty million, three hundred and thirty-three thousand shillings, which is four point two eight percent, and both round it to four point three. The five product changes match to one decimal place, and units and revenue changed by the same percentage because prices did not change.

The weak email also says ninety-seven more bags of beans and sugar at twenty-eight percent of revenue, and both are right. So the difference between the two emails is not accuracy. It is fit, extra claims, and whether the email is finished.

slides.notes:
So what did the brief buy?

These are one run each, and the strong brief asked for each of these things, so the email following them proves little by itself. Left side: a named reader, no placeholder, no advice the data cannot support, an honest line about what the data cannot show, and a shorter email, one hundred and one words against one hundred and fifty-seven, counting everything but the table.

The weak prompt set no length limit and its count includes a closing note. Right side: it did not change the figures, which were right in both. The strong brief did not remove the need to check, and one run each proves little. Notice also that the weak email was not wrong about the numbers.

Its problem was that it was not ready to send, and it said more than the data supports.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_e8449645.png

objects.text: At Nile Valley Foods the review is planned at 20 minutes. Every mistake you find becomes a rule in the brief.

slides.notes:
This is part six of the brief, and it is yours. Find each figure in the data. Recompute totals and percentages, because a sum that looks right is not proof, as you saw in Session 2. Read for claims the data lack, such as a cause for a change or advice that nobody asked for.

In the weak email, that was the advice about stock. And look for what is missing, such as a product or a region left out. At Nile Valley Foods the plan counts twenty minutes for this review. Every mistake you find becomes a rule you add to the brief, so the brief improves each time.

title.text: A complete brief, with your own check beside it

objects.text: 1 Goal
Write the Monday sales email to Sarah Namukasa.
2 Context
I am the sales analyst at Nile Valley Foods, Jinja.
3 Inputs
Use only the figures I paste after this brief.

Invent nothing. Under 150 words plus table.

Subject, table, three sentences, one check, one example.

Not pasted. I find each figure and recount the totals.

If the data cannot explain something, say so.

slides.notes:
Here is a complete brief for the Monday sales email, in the shape of your template. It follows the strong brief we just saw, with part six beside it for you. Read it from the top. The goal names the reader. The inputs are limited to the figures I paste.

The constraints forbid invented numbers, causes and customers. The format fixes the email shape. Part six is a line for me and I do not paste it. Part seven says what to do when the data cannot explain something. Yours will be about this long. Now you decide which part will be hardest.

Goal and reader, inputs, format and length, or what to do when unsure and how you check. Say your choice and a reason. Session 4 deals with that. Whichever you choose, start with that part after the break, while it is fresh.
